stops.name: Old Thargomindah Jail
stops.description: Step inside Thargomindah's Old Jail, a weathered cypress pine fortress from 1930 that once housed rustlers and stock thieves from the wild pastoral frontier — peek through its high barred windows and meet the lifelike figures that bring the outback's rougher days to vivid life.
stops.transcription:
You're standing in front of the Old Thargomindah Jail — built in 1930 from local cypress pine, lined with hardwood, and topped with corrugated iron. Have a look at the windows. They're set high on purpose — this wasn't about ventilation, it was about keeping people in.

But the story of policing here goes back a lot further than this building.

By 1897, the Thargomindah Police Station had a Sub-Inspector, an Acting Sergeant, three Constables, a Native Tracker, and eighteen horses. That's a serious operation for a town of a few hundred people — but this was the pastoral boom. Thousands of sheep and cattle were moving through the district, and where there's livestock, there's rustling.

That was the most common crime out here — stealing sheep and cattle. In a place this remote, the law had to cover around 74,000 square kilometres of the Bulloo Shire. Officers could be called out to ride for days across open country, chasing down stock thieves or tracking missing persons through the mulga.

Inside the cells, you'll meet Sergeant George Schnitzerling and a local character named Sidney Barney. They're animatronic figures, dressed in 1950s gear, having a yarn about Sid's latest trouble — pinching sheep from Norley Station and getting done for obscene language in a public place. Schnitzerling was a real Queensland police officer. Earlier in his career, back in 1932, he was part of the search party in North Queensland after a four-year-old girl was taken by a four-metre crocodile near the Seymour River.

In the jail kitchen, you'll hear from Trixie, the Sergeant's wife, talking about what it was like to live as a policeman's wife out here — the isolation, the heat, and yes, the cooking. She'll also tell you about the Bulloo Downs murder of 1965 — four years after the Schnitzerlings left Thargomindah, three human skulls were discovered on Bulloo Downs Station, just south of town. It shook the whole district.

Step inside the cells if you haven't already. They're small, they're dark, and in a Thargomindah summer — where it regularly hits the high forties — they would have been unbearable.

stops.name: Leahy Historical House
stops.description: The Leahy Historical House, built from Bulloo River mud bricks around 1885, opens its four rooms to transport you straight back to the 1890s, where you can walk through the domestic world of this frontier town during its boom days.
stops.transcription:
The building in front of you is one of the last surviving mud brick structures in Thargomindah. It was built around 1885, and the bricks themselves were made right here — moulded from soil dug off the banks of the Bulloo River and dried in the sun.

The house is named after John Leahy, and to understand Thargomindah, you need to understand this man.

Leahy was born in 1854 in Schull, County Cork, Ireland. He arrived in Queensland and made his way to Thargomindah by 1876, where he opened a general store. Within a few years, he and his brother Patrick owned the Royal Hotel, a cordial factory, part of Thylungra Station, a brewery, and the Thargomindah Herald — the local newspaper that Patrick founded and which, remarkably, had subscribers across Queensland, New South Wales, South Australia, and Victoria.

But Leahy's real legacy is infrastructure. As Chairman of the Bulloo Divisional Board — essentially the local council — he drove the project to drill an artesian bore. Drilling started in 1891, and when they struck water in 1893, the pressure was extraordinary. That bore gave Thargomindah the first reticulated artesian water supply in Australia. And it gave Leahy an even bigger idea — using that water pressure to generate electricity. We'll get to that at the next stop.

Leahy went on to enter the Queensland Parliament in 1893 as the independent member for Bulloo, served as Minister for Railways and Public Works, and in 1907 became Speaker of the House, where he was respected for what was described as his measured handling of parliamentary debate. Not bad for a bloke from a town of 340 people.

In 1912, the house was bought by Sir Sidney Kidman — the cattle king who at his peak controlled more land than any individual in the British Empire. Kidman never lived here. He gave it to his roaming station manager, Jack Watts, known locally as Galloping Jack — because he refused any form of transport other than his horse, and he always rode flat out. Kidman needed a local representative on the Divisional Board, and owning a house in town was a requirement for membership.

The house was continuously lived in until 1995, when the Bulloo Shire Council purchased it for restoration. It's now a museum, open seven days a week, with four rooms of displays covering the Leahy family, station life, and the broader history of the district.

stops.name: Hydro Power Plant
stops.description: In 1893, Thargomindah made world history — this humble outback town harnessed the raw pressure of an underground artesian bore struck at 808 metres to power Australia's first hydroelectric street lights, making it just the third town on Earth to shine with electricity from flowing water.
stops.transcription:
This is where a tiny outback town did something that put it alongside London and Paris.

When the artesian bore was drilled in 1893, water came up from nearly 800 metres underground at 84 degrees Celsius. The flow was enormous — around 1,300 cubic metres per day — and the natural pressure was immense. John Leahy and the Bulloo Divisional Board saw an opportunity that no one else in the country had tried.

They took a generator that had originally been powered by a steam engine, coupled it to a turbine, and installed the whole thing inside a casing made from a water tank. Those tanks had an interesting history of their own — they'd been hauled to Thargomindah from Bourke by bullock wagon to supply drinking water before the bore was drilled.

The original water wheel was built locally. It was later replaced with a Pelton wheel — a turbine specifically designed to convert the energy of a high-pressure water jet into rotational power — and then upgraded again with a Triumph Pelton wheel, which is the one you can see on display now. The original locally made wheel is in the Queensland Powerhouse Museum in Brisbane.

In 1898, the street lights of Thargomindah came on.

A town of around 340 people, a thousand kilometres from Brisbane, in the remote south-west corner of Queensland — lit its streets with hydroelectric power before Sydney, before Melbourne, before any other town in the country. According to the Sydney Bulletin at the time, only London and Paris had done it first. That made Thargomindah the third place in the world to have hydroelectric street lighting.

The plant ran continuously for over fifty years, until 1951, when diesel generators took over. The town eventually connected to the state power grid via Cunnamulla in 1988 — almost a century after this bore-powered plant first threw light onto Dowling Street.

The plant has been restored and is believed to be the oldest working hydroelectric unit in Australia — and possibly the world. What you're looking at isn't a replica. This is the real thing.
